result.markdown: --- title: "01 · Introduction" subtitle: "Week 1" --- ::: {.guiding-q} What is a statistical model? ::: ## In this session - Why statistics in CBB research: description, estimation, inference, prediction - A statistical model = a **systematic part** (what we expect) + a **random part** (how observations scatter around it) - The linear model as the common language of this course - From research question to model: response, predictors, unit of observation - Course overview and workflow (R projects, Quarto, reproducibility) ::: {.key-terms} **Key terms:** [Assumptions (of the linear model)](../../glossary.qmd#assumptions), [Residuals](../../glossary.qmd#residuals) ::: ## Learning goals After this session you can - explain what a statistical model is and which parts it has, - write a simple linear model as an equation and translate it into words, - set up an R project with a Quarto document for your analyses. ## Simulate first Before we fit anything, we write down a model and let it generate data. Here: body mass (kg) increases with age (years), plus random variation. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(1) n <- 50 age <- runif(n, 1, 10) b0 <- 3; b1 <- 0.8; sigma <- 1.5 # the "true" model mass <- b0 + b1 * age + rnorm(n, 0, sigma) plot(age, mass, pch = 19, col = "#1b6f8a", xlab = "Age (years)", ylab = "Body mass (kg)") abline(b0, b1, col = "#c0392b", lwd = 2) # the systematic part ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](01-introduction_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-1-1.png){width=975} ::: ::: ::: {.box} **Systematic part:** $\mu_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot \text{age}_i$ **Random part:** $y_i \sim \text{Normal}(\mu_i, \sigma)$ ::: ## Materials ::: {.materials} - Slides coming soon - R script coming soon - Exercises coming soon ::: ## Reading - Gelman, A., Hill, J., & Vehtari, A. (2020). *Regression and other stories*, ch. 1. Cambridge University Press.
